subject: workflow using nimbleModel(calculate = T/F) and model$calculate()

messages.author: bed9858844040a0b
messages.subject: workflow using nimbleModel(calculate = T/F) and model$calculate()
parts:
Following initial conversations and guidance from folks here, I have developed a Nimble workflow as follows:

1. Write model
2. Use `nimbleModel()` to define and build the model
3. Run `model$calculate()` to check that I get a number for the log-likelihood and thus the model is fully initialized, specified, and is set to start in a defined portion of parameter space
4. Initiate sampling

During step 2, I am noticing "Running calculate on model" in the R console, which made me wonder if step 3 is duplicating what is already done in step 2. I then searched here and found this post, where Perry advises the questioner to set calculate = FALSE when running nimbleModel(). I have two questions:

1. Is it possible to get the calculated overall deviance from the model object produced by `nimbleModel()` without having to run Step 3?
2. Alternatively, should I always be setting `nimbleModel(calculate = FALSE)` to avoid wasting time on what I will be doing in step 3?
3. Moreover, in line 40 of my function that parallelizes Nimble here, should I be setting calculate = FALSE to avoid wasting time when compiling the model, or is this in fact a needed step when setting up the model prior to compiling samplers?

messages.author: bed9858844040a0b
messages.subject: Re: workflow using nimbleModel(calculate = T/F) and model$calculate()
parts: Thought about this some more and tested this myself using the pump model in the manual. My code and results are attached. It seems that I get the exact same set of estimates regardless of whether I set calculate = TRUE or FALSE. Model build time seems to be a bit faster with calculate = FALSE, but the run time ended up being a second slower for at least one trial. There is variation in the model build times and run times each time I do it, but it seems like there might not be much to gain setting calculate = FALSE. I'm guessing if I don't calculate at the `nimbleModel`, calculate happens later in another subsequent function in this workflow. Would be great to get confirmation or know if I'm missing something in my assessment.

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: workflow using nimbleModel(calculate = T/F) and model$calculate()
parts:
Hi Quresh,

Thanks for these messages and I suspect others encounter similar questions about what is really going on.

Yes, your step 3 is redundant with a call to model$calculate() that is done internally to step 2 (nimbleModel) unless "calculate=FALSE".

The main difference is that when nimbleModel does model$calculate(), it can issue a warning if any steps result in NaN or +/- Inf. Of course, it is just a warning because there is no requirement for the model to be fully and validly initialized when it is built by nimbleModel. Otherwise it is pretty much equivalent to have either "calculate=TRUE" or to have "calculate=FALSE" and then do model$calculate() yourself. Neither is necessary prior to compileNimble.

I don't think there is a way to get the return value of model$calculate() (the total log probability) when it is run inside nimbleModel.

If a user wants to save time in nimbleModel, setting "calculate=FALSE" can help, especially for large models.

If one is going to immediately run model$calculate() after nimbleModel, that will incur a similar time cost as having calculate=TRUE in nimbleModel, although perhaps not quite as much.

There is no need to do model$calculate() at all (inside or outside nimbleModel) prior to compileNimble. model$calculate() will set values of log probabilities of stochastic nodes and values of deterministic nodes, but these don't need to be set in order for compileNimble to work.

A subtle point is that once you have a compiled model (say Cmodel), then Cmodel$calculate() will run faster than model$calculate() but still much slower than model$calculate() inside a compiled nimbleFunction (which will always use the compiled model). That is because if you run Cmodel$calculate() in R, the iteration over model nodes is still being managed from R, with each node's calculation being done via a call to the compiled model. If you have model$calculate() in a compiled nimbleFunction, the iteration over model nodes is being done in C++, which will be typically much much faster.

I hope that clarifies things a bit. Let us know further questions.

Perry
